market_context: United States/international; refrigerated high-protein puddings and dairy desserts.
title: Protein Pudding: What It Is, How Much Protein It Usually Has, and How to Read the Label

seo.title: Protein Pudding: Protein, Sugar, and How to Read the Label
seo.meta_description: Many 200 g protein puddings provide about 20 g of protein, but the category has no single recipe. Compare protein per cup, sugars, sweeteners, fat, lactose, and ingredients.
seo.search_intent: Understand what protein pudding is, how much protein a typical cup can provide, and how to evaluate the label beyond the high-protein claim.

excerpt: Protein pudding is not a standardized recipe. It is usually a thick dairy dessert made with milk plus added or concentrated milk proteins. Current 200 g products commonly provide about 20 g of protein per cup, or roughly 10 g per 100 g, but sugar, sweeteners, fat, and serving size vary by brand.
content_html:
Protein pudding is essentially a creamy dessert formulated to deliver substantially more protein than a typical pudding or custard. The base is often milk or skim milk with added milk protein, casein, whey, or another protein ingredient, plus thickeners and flavoring.

There is no universal formula. Several current 200 g products provide 20 g protein per cup, which equals about 10 g per 100 g. That is common enough to be a useful reference, but the number still needs to be checked on the label.

Twenty grams per cup is common, but serving size matters

Current products from brands such as Arla and Ehrmann list roughly 10 g protein per 100 g and 20 g in a 200 g cup. That makes the category convenient for someone looking for a snack or dessert that contributes a meaningful amount of protein.

Do not confuse “20 g per pot” with “10 g per 100 g.” They describe the same concentration on different bases. Protein per package tells you what the food adds to your day if you eat the whole cup; protein per 100 g is better for comparing products sold in different package sizes.

Where the protein comes from

Many products rely on milk plus added milk proteins. Casein and whey provide essential amino acids and also help create the dense texture when combined with heat processing and stabilizers.

Formulas differ. Some use milk protein concentrate, others whey or casein fractions, and some include additional amino acids or non-dairy proteins. The ingredient list is the place to verify the source.

If your goal is simply total protein, grams per serving matter most. If allergies, lactose, vegan eating, or protein source matter, the ingredient list is just as important.

No added sugar does not mean sugar-free

Dairy pudding can contain naturally occurring lactose even when no sucrose or syrup has been added. Products treated with lactase may still list sugars because lactose has been split into glucose and galactose.

Many high-protein desserts also use sweeteners such as sucralose, stevia glycosides, erythritol, or acesulfame potassium. Whether you prefer those is a separate question; the key is not to interpret “no added sugar” as zero carbohydrate or zero sweetness.

Protein does not describe the entire dessert

Two puddings with the same 20 g protein can differ in calories, saturated fat, sugars, sodium, sweetener system, and toppings. Some current examples sit around 70–80 calories per 100 g with relatively low fat, while richer versions can be more energy-dense.

Compare like with like. If this is an everyday snack, review protein, calories, saturated fat, sugars, and ingredients. If it is an occasional dessert, taste and satisfaction may matter more than optimizing every number.

Does protein pudding replace yogurt, a shake, or a meal?

It can easily replace a snack or dessert. It may also contribute calcium and other dairy nutrients, but it usually contains little fiber and a narrow range of foods.

A meal may still need fruit, whole grains, nuts, or other foods depending on context. Likewise, a protein pudding is not automatically superior to Greek yogurt, skyr, cottage cheese, or a shake if those options provide similar protein and fit your preferences better.

How to read the package quickly

Start with protein grams per cup and confirm whether the package is one serving. Next compare calories and sugars per 100 g or equivalent serving. Check saturated fat and sodium, then scan the ingredient list for protein source, sweeteners, and thickeners.

The practical rule: protein pudding can be a convenient way to get around 20 g protein in one small cup, but the word “protein” does not replace label reading. Use per-serving protein to plan your diet and a standardized basis to compare competing products.

faq.question: How much protein is in protein pudding?
faq.answer: Many current 200 g products provide about 20 g, or roughly 10 g per 100 g, but brands vary.

faq.question: Does no added sugar mean protein pudding is sugar-free?
faq.answer: No. Dairy naturally contains lactose, and products may use non-sugar sweeteners while still containing naturally occurring sugars.

faq.question: Can protein pudding replace a meal?
faq.answer: Not automatically. It can provide substantial protein but usually lacks the food variety and fiber of a complete meal.
